1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6.name: Petrov's Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6.background: First popularised by the Russian player Alexander Petrov in the mid-nineteenth century; in recognition of the early investigations by Petrov and Carl Jaenisch it is also called the Russian Game, the predominant name in some countries. World champions Smyslov, Petrosian, Karpov and Kramnik have all adopted it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5.strategy: Takes the pawn that Black left undefended. Black cannot simply retake on e4 at once, because the open e-file gives White tactics against the king, so the knight on e5 has to be driven off first. The game stays close to level: White has the first-move initiative, Black a very solid position.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5.name: Petrov's Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5.background: Of White's two main third moves it is the more popular, ahead of 3.d4.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4.strategy: Attacks the centre at once instead of grabbing a pawn, and lets Black choose which pawn to take. White opens the game early for fast development and activity, but the pawn exchanges that follow leave Black with a sound, roughly equal game.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4.background: Carl Jaenisch credited Alexander Petrov with the move, and Wilhelm Steinitz recommended it in his Modern Chess Instructor (1889), playing it three times against Pillsbury at St Petersburg 1895–96 for two wins and a draw. It came into vogue in the 1990s, when players such as Kasparov and Ivanchuk adopted it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Qe2.strategy: Defends e4 with the queen, a solid-looking but awkward way: the queen blocks the f1 bishop, so the kingside cannot develop smoothly, and White has threatened nothing. Black can develop freely and fight for the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 by developing a piece and avoids the sharper lines of this defence. It is sound but modest: Black answers by developing the other knight and reaches a symmetrical, level position in which White has little to claim.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3.name: Petrov's Defence: Three Knights Game

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4.strategy: Aims the bishop at f7 at once, but leaves the e4 pawn undefended. Black can simply take it, and White has only a gambit to show for the pawn; or Black declines and reaches an ordinary balanced game. Either way White has gained little for the early commitment.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4.name: Petrov's Defence: Italian Variation

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 Nxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn that White left undefended and so makes White prove the gambit. The knight stands exposed on e4, but Black has several sound ways to defend it and either keep the extra pawn or return it on good terms.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4.strategy: The main reply: Black takes the e4 pawn, and since White can retake on e5, the pawns are simply traded. The advanced knight needs support, but the symmetrical positions that follow are the soundest way to meet the early central strike, and give White at best a slight initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn on d4 and keeps the extra pawn for now, but opens the e-file with the king still in the centre. White regains the pawn with tempo by attacking the knight, so Black spends time retreating. Sound and playable, but more passive than the main reply.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 d5.strategy: Meets the central strike with the d-pawn, which hands the decision about what to capture on e5 back to White. Solid and symmetrical, but it gives White the choice of structure: play usually transposes into the main lines, so Black gains nothing from the changed order.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 d5.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack, Symmetrical Variation

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the other knight, the most common and best-regarded reply. Both sides now have both knights out, and the game takes a symmetrical, classical course that avoids the lines special to this defence. Black is solid and level, with White having little to claim.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6.strategy: Attacks the knight on e5 and so drives it away before Black retakes the pawn. This is the sound way to equalise: once the knight has left the e-file, Black can take on e4 without running into tactics. The game is close to level, with White holding a small initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4.strategy: Retakes at once, but the open e-file punishes it: the queen attacks e4 from e2, and a knight move uncovers a discovered check, so the natural-looking ...Nf6 loses the queen to Nc6+. Black has to find exact moves to survive and still ends up worse.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6.strategy: Offers the e-pawn for an open d-file, an active c8 bishop and an immediate attack on e4, aimed at White's kingside. If White replies calmly, Black has no real compensation for the pawn, but many natural-looking moves for White run into tactics.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Qe2 Nc6.strategy: A natural developing reply: the knight guards e5 and joins the fight for d4, while White's queen, standing in front of its own bishop, has nothing to attack. Black gets easy development and can aim for the centre.
